technique.how: With the patient at rest and unaware of being observed (for example while appearing to take the pulse), count chest or abdominal excursions for a full 60 seconds; do not extrapolate from 15 seconds. Record the rate, and note pattern (Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes) and use of accessory muscles.
technique.prerequisites: Patient at rest for several minutes; not talking; not immediately after exertion or pain.

interpretation.positive_finding: Respiratory rate above 24-25/min sustained at rest; indicates cardiopulmonary, metabolic or septic stress and is a component of qSOFA/CURB-65.
interpretation.negative_finding: Normal rate (12-20/min) together with normal temperature and heart rate substantially lowers probability of pneumonia (pooled LR- about 0.24); normal rate does not exclude pulmonary embolism.
interpretation.pitfalls: Monitor-derived and 15-second counts are inaccurate; anxiety, pain, fever and acidosis all raise the rate. In the elderly and immunocompromised, tachypnea may be the only sign of pneumonia or sepsis.
interpretation.changes_what: RR >24 with fever/cough: obtain CXR and assess severity; normal vital signs plus normal lung exam make CAP unlikely enough to defer imaging in low-risk outpatients.

estimates.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia (any abnormal vital sign: temperature, heart rate or respiratory rate)
estimates.population: Outpatient adults and adolescents with acute respiratory infection or cough; 4 studies

estimates.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia (absence of abnormal vital signs)
estimates.population: Adults with clinically suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED)
estimates.quote: decreased most by the absence of abnormal vital signs (LR- = 0.25, 95% CI = 0.11 to 0.48)

sources.citation: Marchello CS, Ebell MH, Dale AP, Harvill ET, Shen Y, Whalen CC. Signs and symptoms that rule out community-acquired pneumonia in outpatient adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Am Board Fam Med. 2019;32(2):234-247.
Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia: a meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
Metlay JP, Kapoor WN, Fine MJ. Does this patient have community-acquired pneumonia? Diagnosing pneumonia by history and physical examination. JAMA. 1997;278(17):1440-1445.
Chunilal SD, Eikelboom JW, Attia J, et al. Does this patient have pulmonary embolism? JAMA. 2003;290(21):2849-2858.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal respiratory rate to exclude pulmonary embolism, sepsis or metabolic acidosis; do not rely on nurse-charted or monitor rates for decisions.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: RR >30/min, or tachypnea with hypotension, hypoxemia or altered mental status, indicates severe illness (sepsis, severe CAP, PE); escalate and obtain blood gas.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No reliability statistic for a 60-second count located in the sources viewed; Marchello 2020 notes individual studies used different thresholds (>20, >25/min).

extraction_notes: No accessible source gave an isolated LR for RR >24-25/min: the Metlay 1997 JAMA RCE (which tabulates RR >25 from Diehr 1984/Gennis 1989) and the Ebell 2020 meta-analysis are not open access, and their abstracts report only composite vital-sign results. Both entered estimates are therefore for the COMPOSITE 'any abnormal vital sign (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate)' from Marchello 2020 Table 3 (PMC7422644; RR thresholds >20 or >25 by study, see Appendix B2) and Ebell 2020 abstract; status set to partially_quantified. Chunilal 2003 PE RCE is cited for context only (abstract gives no tachypnea accuracy).
